reading.body:
Carlyle Thorsen is named on 59 AI lobbying filings, and the clients behind them are concentrated in entertainment, copyright, and news media rather than in compute or data centers.

The client list runs from the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees and the Directors Guild of America to the Copyright Clearance Center, the International Trademark Association, and Comcast. Bria Artificial Intelligence, an AI company, appears with 7 filings, and the American Society of Composers, Authors, and Publishers appears through a separate advocacy firm. Seven bills are named on filings from 2025 or later, all of them Senate or House measures identified only by number here. The pattern is AI policy fought over rights, credit, and compensation, which is the layer above the physical build.

That matters because the AI debate is often described as a contest over chips, land, and electricity. This record shows a parallel and well funded effort aimed at the rules governing training data, likeness, and ownership of creative work. Those rules determine what AI systems are permitted to learn from and what they owe the people whose work they absorb. The clients with the most filings are the parties with the most to lose from permissive training rules.

The data does not say what position any client took, what any bill would do, or whether the lobbying changed an outcome. It covers one lobbyist, one firm, and filings that mention AI, so it is a slice of a much larger influence map. The prior government positions listed are disclosures required by the Lobbying Disclosure Act, not findings about conduct.

summary: Carlyle Thorsen is named as a lobbyist on 59 Lobbying Disclosure Act filing(s) about AI held by this site. The firms, clients and AI bills on those filings are below. LDA lobbyist id 51449. A different lobbyist with the same name has a separate page.
